Tabletop Object Collection: From 3D Model to Final Render

Role3D Modelling and Visualisation
TimelineJun 2026 to Aug 2026
ToolsRhino, Grasshopper
OutputRendered scene and drawing set
The Brief

Build a small collection of objects from scratch in Rhino and take them all the way to two finished deliverables: a staged render showing how they look, and a dimensioned drawing set showing how they would be made. The point was to cover the full pipeline rather than stop at a model that looks good in the viewport.

Five objects, five different modelling problems: a piece of furniture, a vessel with parts joined onto it, a vessel with surface detail, an organic form that flat surfaces cannot describe, and a form generated by a rule rather than drawn by hand.

01 · Table

The top started as a rectangle and was resolved three ways to compare corner treatments: sharp corners, corners cut with a Boolean difference, and a rounded corner rectangle. The rounded version carried forward.

The legs were the real exercise. I built them four ways from the same guiding curves, using an extrusion, a loft, a single rail sweep and a two rail sweep, then compared which gave the most control over the silhouette. The wireframe view shows all four sitting together. The two rail sweep won because it let me drive the curve from two directions at once.

02 · Vase with Handle and Spout

This one began as a sphere, cut down with trims, splits and a Boolean difference until it read as a vessel. I then tested wall thickness properly: offsetting as a closed solid, offsetting as an open surface, and offsetting with the control points moved to create deliberately uneven thickness, so I could see what each approach does to the finished object.

The handle and spout were built as swept surfaces along their own spine curves, trimmed back into the body, then joined with blend surfaces so the transitions are smooth rather than creased. Everything closes into a single watertight solid, which is what makes it manufacturable rather than just a picture of a vase. This is the object the drawing set documents.

03 · Patterned Vase

A profile curve revolved into a body, then rebuilt so the surface had even spacing to work with. The pattern was drawn flat, patched into a tile and arrayed across a grid.

The interesting step is getting a flat pattern onto a curved body. I unrolled the surface to a flat reference, laid the array onto it, then flowed it back onto the revolved form. Because the vase closes on itself, I handled the two sides of the seam separately so the pattern meets cleanly instead of tearing. Around four hundred tiles were cut into the body, then the interior was offset and blended to close it back into a solid. I built the pattern in two variants, a diamond and a triangle, so the motif could be swapped without rebuilding the vase.

04 · SubD Form

Surface modelling struggles with organic shapes, so this one was built in SubD instead. It starts as a box, edited first in the front view and then in the top view against orthographic reference, then developed outward: the head, the central fin, the side fins, the tail and the smaller details, with parts detached and rejoined where the topology needed it, and a bend applied at the end.

On the reference: this was a modelling study built against existing photographic reference rather than an original concept of my own. What it demonstrates is SubD topology and the curvature analysis used to check the surface, not the invention of the form.

05 · Parametric Study

The last form was not drawn directly. I built a Grasshopper definition that sweeps a profile along a curve and arrays it around an axis, so every copy updates when the input curve moves. Changing one number rebuilds the whole object.

It is a small definition, but it covers the shift from modelling one object by hand to describing a rule that generates many, which is the difference between a shape and a system.

06 · Final Output 1: The Drawing Set

The render shows how an object looks. The drawing shows how it gets made. I took the vase with the handle and spout and generated flat projections from the 3D model in top, front and right views, dimensioned them at 738mm length, 233mm width and 490mm height, labelled the handle and spout with leaders, and placed everything on a sheet with detail views, a border and a title block.

This is the deliverable that would go to whoever builds the thing, and it is the half of the pipeline most modelling exercises skip.

07 · Materials and Finish

Every object was modelled in the same neutral white, so the scene was where they got their character. I chose four finishes that behave differently under the same light: walnut for the top, a gloss magenta, a matte grey, and a translucent red.

The pairing was deliberate. Gloss on the patterned vase catches a highlight on every raised tile, which makes the relief read from across the room, where a matte finish would have flattened it. The matte grey does the opposite and lets the large vase hold its silhouette without competing. The translucent red was the one that did not work: it swallows the SubD surface I spent the longest building, and if I reran the scene I would make that piece opaque and lift it off the tabletop.

What I Took From It

Most of the difficulty was not making shapes, it was keeping them valid. Offsetting a wall, blending a handle into a body, flowing a pattern across a seam: each of these can look correct in the viewport while leaving the object open or self intersecting underneath. Checking that everything closed into a solid at each stage was what separated a model that renders from a model that could be made.

Ending on a drawing set rather than an image changed how I modelled. Knowing a dimension would have to sit on the geometry later made me build cleaner geometry from the start.
